sections.h:
The hurricane of the Enlightenment

Rome in the first half of the nineteenth century still lacks a complete history. Its broad lines, most notable events and leading figures are known, but it lacks a unified account and above all significant detail. The studies that do exist, and there are several,[1] show, as for other periods, a concern to bring out the political, religious, military, economic, cultural and administrative context, but they do not always bring out the links and supports, the secondary figures who contributed, often decisively, alongside the great figures of the time. As research and monographs bring to light new pieces of the period’s mosaic, its lines, colours and components take clearer shape: causes, coincidences and effects are discovered and studied, as well as those who conceived or carried things out. What remains to be brought out is the ultimate why, the underlying motive, which comes from the true protagonist of history, almost always officially ignored: God. For the period of our story too, the saying holds: “Man proposes and God disposes.”

This period, full of ferment and violent upheaval, of-

1 Cf. the rich bibliography given by MARTINA in “Pio IX (1846-1850)”, Rome 1974.

ten catastrophic, not unlike that in other States of the Italian Peninsula and Europe, especially the Kingdom of Sardinia, France, Austria and Germany, felt the effects of the great upheavals in thought and action. The collapse that followed the French Revolution favoured the overweening power of Bonaparte, who held two Popes prisoner and in exile, one of whom died there.[2] His overthrow through the Emperor’s defeat, imprisonment and death cleared the way for the Restoration, and at the same time gave new strength and influence to the great powers of central Europe, eager to appear as champions of the Church so as to have a presence in her State, and to the official or secret channels of the ideas fermenting within them. The appearance was support and defence; the reality was often the opposite, with a common source in the Enlightenment, which spread from Germany, England and France under various names from the second half of the eighteenth century, whether called encyclopaedism or free thought, presented as rationalism, secularism or materialism. It was, at root, “modern” opposition to the dominant traditional culture and civilization: an explanation of the world, of man and his destiny opposed to the Christian one; and

“even before the revolutionary storm gathered its clouds over the sky of Rome,” observes a specialist in eighteenth-century Rome, “the capital of the Catholic world was not a culturally closed environment

sheltered from every devastating whirlwind… The ‘Europe des lumières’ certainly did not dazzle the eyes and minds of the Romans, but they too saw some bright flashes on the horizon, and some were moved to consider how much of the new ideas could be reconciled with Christian tradition, while others began to drift away from it.”[3]

From isolated avant-garde circles and elites, subversion spread subtly through the nobility, those in power and the bourgeoisie, and then infected the professions, the administrative class and the masses. In some cases part of the clergy too was infected. If in France, with Voltaire, it led to the Revolution, the first and typical one of the series that would follow, elsewhere it caused other upheavals, all in the name of “Reason”, which was supposed to rule unchallenged in every field of life and culture. The spirit of Enlightenment rationalism, scientistic and positivist, fighting for the complete emancipation of reason from Faith, aimed to subvert all religious faith, especially Christian faith, the order of nature and grace, spirit and matter, God and man, trying to undermine their foundations so as to put man in a central, absolute position, with no reference to his origin in and dependence on God and his Revelation. This meant destroying the supernatural, beginning with the centrality of God and Christ; at most, rationalizing religion in terms of pure reason and critical, epistemological and scientific inquiry, but outside Faith and dogma, Providence and Christian precepts, the sacraments and Catholic morality, the duty of virtue and the avoidance of sin. Indeed it meant all-out war on Religion and its representatives: popes, bishops,

3 VITTORIO EMANUELE GIUNTELLA, Roma nel Settecento, Bologna 1971, pp. 130-131.

priests, religious in general and committed laity; hence anticlericalism and hostility to friars at every level, beginning with the Society of Jesus, the Church’s vanguard. It meant war on miracles and contempt for contemplation, as for any activity attentive to God and his Word or cultivating a vital vertical relationship with him, whether in inner worship or in its public and social expression.

The move was gradual, from a vague rationalist deism, conceiving God as a separate mind, detached from and indifferent to the world, to a pantheism that, claiming to divinize values, empties them, and sinks into the most aberrant and violent atheism. It is the story of humanity, which whenever it turns away from God turns against itself and becomes less human: man once again a wolf to man.

Reason opposed to religion degenerates into a religion of reason, which excludes any criteria of judgement foreign to it. Hence absolute independence from all revealed truth and every ethical principle it dictates, and the isolation of man, who deludes himself that he is the centre of everything while he is at the mercy of the cleverest, the strongest and the most domineering; and the struggle of man against man is renewed, ever more tragic.

But if the signs of the times were frightening, the signs of renewal grew stronger.

In the eye of the cyclone

In Rome at the time we are speaking of, life seemed to go on as usual, although the cyclone could be felt in the air. The opposition of the new bourgeoisie (businessmen, professionals, the newly rich), the schemes and ambitions of Austria and France, and the struggles of the secret societies fanned unrest and rekindled revolt. Beside churches and palaces, ruins and monuments, backing onto charitable institutions and monasteries or lined up irregularly along squares and more or less straight or winding streets, houses and hovels alternated with craftsmen’s workshops. High-ranking prelates and nobles, but also simple priests and humble religious, and many common people and servants lived and worked in the shadow of the Church, as if protected by its symbol, the great dome. Salons and artists’ studios were open to the sons of Italian and foreign families, and artists and scholars, local and foreign, displayed their talent there. So with the names of cardinals and princes and distinguished ladies, many of them of foreign birth and language, were intertwined those of guests representing one branch or another of the sciences and arts, who came here from every country as an obligatory stage or goal of their experience.[4] Stendhal and Goethe, Chateaubriand, Ozanam and Ampère, Mommsen and Gregorovius, Rossini, Liszt and Bizet, Acton and Scott, Witte, Taine and Weimar, Human, Lotzbeck and Baudelaire, to name some of the best known, were among them.

Inns and eating houses, on the other hand, were frequented by ordinary workers, vendors from Campo Porcino and the neighbourhood markets, humble carters and tenant farmers come to their landlords’ houses.

Some lived on private incomes, but others, if they wanted to make a living with some dignity, had to work very hard. There was work, certainly not in industry or trade, but in service of one kind or another, as guides or cicerones for lovers of antiquities and art, or in providing lodging for travellers and pilgrims interested not only in the religious side of the City. There was certainly no shortage of poor people, poor in everything; devout and charitable people cared for them, but

4 FIORELLA BARTOCCINI, Lettere di Michelangelo Caetani duca di Sermoneta, Roma 1974, p. 7.

it was never enough. In the Monti district, one of the poorest working-class areas of the City, run-down since the days of the “Suburra”, even “the Saint of the poor”, the French pilgrim Benedict Joseph Labre, found a wandering home; on the evening of 16 April 1783 he would collapse dying on the steps of the parish church of the Madonna dei Monti and find his last bed in a nearby lodging in the adjoining Via dei Serpenti.

Gendarmes and palace guards had their hands full, not only preventing disorders caused by agents of secret societies and exiles, who found it easy to slip into the Pope’s peaceful lands, but also dealing with the last notorious brigands, such as the followers of “Gasbarrone”,[5] though more in the rest of Lazio than in the capital.

The Papacy and the Curia gave meaning and tone to Roman life, and neither the biting satires pinned to the torso of Pasquino or the statues of Marforio and the Babuino, nor Belli’s sonnets[6] and criticism of the system, even from some aristocrats, were enough to make it revolutionary, or even constitutional and secular. That would

Nevertheless, in the introduction to those […] [main text continues:] come under Pius IX, when the clash with the real liberal, Masonic and Carbonari aims, stirred up by followers of Mazzini and radicals, by sincere Italians and by class agitators, would turn into explosion and open rebellion.

Rome, however, was meanwhile in the eye of the cyclone. Around it the wind of the Enlightenment hurricane whirled furiously, but nothing disturbed its true meaning and purpose amid the roar of the storm. Yet there was no lack of attacks and events aimed at undermining not one but both powers. The struggle brewing on the banks of the Tiber was between two utterly different worlds: life inspired by Faith and life practically separated from it. At its origin was the “philosophical fanaticism” of the great minds of the Enlightenment, which supplied ideology and strength to the forces that would work more concretely in the secrecy of Masonic lodges and the circles of the “Illuminati”.[7] The Church and the Papacy, Christian Rome, pivot, bulwark and centre of Catholicism, became their inevitable target and would remain so at every turn of the century. But there is One who watches and governs with the power of the Spirit, who raises up or leads here minds enlightened by a clearer and sounder light, and generous hearts ready to serve the truth that saves.

The rise and spread of these errors and of the movements that sought to apply them were met by the seeds of a religious spirit that held firm under the influence of excellent masters of spirituality and mission- [note 6 continued:] published in his lifetime, he describes the origin of his verses: “Every district of Rome, every one of its citizens from the middle class down, has supplied me with episodes for my drama, in which the shopkeeper will appear as well as the servant, and the naked beggar will show himself between the credulous little woman and the fierce carter. So, bringing together the various classes of the whole people and making each one say what he knows, thinks and does, I have summed up the mass of customs and opinions of these common people, among whom the strangest contradictions stand out” (cf. GIUSEPPE GIOACCHINO BELLI, Tutti i sonetti romaneschi, 5 vols., Rome 1964-65, I, p. 79). 7 GIUNTELLA, Roma nel Settecento, p. 185.

aries of God’s Word, such as Saint Leonard of Port Maurice and Saint Paul of the Cross, Saint Alphonsus M. de’ Liguori and Saint Vincent Strambi, Saint John Baptist de Rossi, Saint Gaspar del Bufalo and Saint Vincent Pallotti, to mention only the best known.[8] With repeated calls, here and elsewhere, to the truths of the Gospel, the wisdom of the Cross, the need for conversion and penance, and humble, generous service of the Church and souls, they built a strong dam against religious decadence and compromise. “The moral and spiritual poverty of eighteenth-

9 Cf. NASELLI, La cura pastorale e la spiritualità in Italia nella prima metà dell’Ottocento, in “Restaurazione e crisi liberale” (cit.), p. 111.

Saint PAUL of the Cross (Ovada 1694 - Rome 1775). From a life of intense asceticism on Monte Argentario, alternating with preaching on the Passion to the people, he devoted himself with his Clerks Regular of the Passion to popular missions and preaching to religious, especially in Lazio and Tuscany.

Saint ALPHONSUS M. de’ LIGUORI (Naples 1696 - Pagani 1787). He first exercised his priestly ministry in the poorest districts, organizing and preaching missions to the people. He was Bishop of S. Agata de’ Goti, and pastoral too in his literary work and writings on moral theology. His apostolate was supported and extended by his religious, the “Redemptorists”.

Saint VINCENT M. STRAMBI (Civitavecchia 1745 - Rome 1824): Passionist and bishop, preacher of Missions and Spiritual Exercises. He was formed on the great doctors ancient and modern, from Saint John Chrysostom to Saint Alphonsus M. de’ Liguori. He was an outstanding director of souls, some of whom attained heroic holiness.

Saint GASPAR del BUFALO (Rome 1786-1837) [the original reads 1755]. As foretold by the Servant of God Sr. M. Agnese of the Incarnate Word, an enclosed Minim nun, he founded the Missionaries of the Most Precious Blood. He spread God’s Word through popular Missions, especially in Roman churches, among them S. Andrea delle Fratte and the Chiesa Nuova, and in Lazio.

Saint JOHN BAPTIST de ROSSI (Voltaggio 1698 - Rome 1764). A diocesan priest wholly devoted to catechetical instruction and the spiritual and charitable care of the humblest and most suffering, he spent over forty years in assiduous priestly ministry, especially at S. Maria in Cosmedin.

Saint VINCENT PALLOTTI (Rome 1795-1850). Founder of the Society of the Catholic Apostolate (Pallottines), he worked for the spread of the faith and works of charity, spiritual direction and the care of workers. We shall return to him, since he was a very dear friend of our Clausi. [main text continues:] century Rome and the contradiction between faith and morals provoked, under the influence of these ‘great Spirits’, a deeper and purer religious longing present in that century, which sought to awaken dulled and drowsy spirits, calling them to a more decided and consistent commitment to Christian life.”[9]

So one should not think of this period only in terms of the well-known popular portraits by Pinelli and Belli. Far more serious and dramatic realities formed the axis around which religious and civil life revolved at every level of Roman society.

Sound Catholic doctrine, opposed to rigorism, and an equally sound ascetic formation marked by clear fidelity to the Faith, to the Church and to the teaching of the Vicar of Christ, spread through Missions and Exercises for the people and through the devout practices of night as well as day adoration and the Way of the Cross,[10] formed the first dam against the rising tide of the Enlightenment. From this flowering sprang a garland of chosen souls who, by explicit appeal to the supernatural, expressed in faith and works, brought about a dynamic awakening of Christian, Catholic religious consciousness deep within individuals and families. So when everything seemed swept away in the institutions and structures whose visible centre was Rome and the Pope, the Church’s vitality and fruitfulness became more evident, to which the Saints and the Catholic educational and social works of the second half of the nineteenth century would be linked. But their roots lie in the first half of the century.

The documented events of the Rue du Bac in Paris, of S. Andrea delle Fratte in Rome and of La Salette near

10 The Way of the Cross at the Colosseum was begun by Saint Leonard of Port Maurice. The cross carried there, going round the interior as through successive “Stations”, was kept at the nearest parish, Saint Francis of Paola.

Grenoble[11] confirm the supernatural breaking into the human reality of a century troubled by unrest and error. At the same time spiritual vitality, the priority of faith and relationship with the supernatural were nourished by devotion, sacramental life and Christian commitment, which strengthened assent to religious truths and the corresponding way of life. Spiritual direction and everything aimed at inner progress and outward witness, following the example of the Lord’s Passion and the Most Precious Blood, the Sacred Heart of Jesus, the Virgin and the Saints, spurred people to an ever more consistent life of faith in works. This was promoted in Rome and the Papal States by a new band of souls raised up by God or led here by the paths of his Providence, who were formed in a religious Romanness that is less a citizenship than freedom in obedience to Christ and his Church, where people are still taught, as Seneca said, that “to obey God is freedom”;[12] it is catholicity, universality open to all peoples, and transcendence. They were eminent prelates, such as Cardinal Carlo Odescalchi,[13] and priests, men and women religious distinguished only by outstanding virtue, and simple lay faithful of most edifying inner life and observance. Fragrant petals of this garland of men of God and devoted daughters of the Church were, besides those already mentioned (Strambi, Del Bufalo and Pallotti), Clausi, Merlini, Canori Mora, Sr. Agnese of the Incarnate Word, Taigi, Sanna and a hundred others.[14]

The meaning of a presence and its beginning

Bernardo Clausi was one of those religious priests who joined others of the Roman clergy whose deeds and merits are still almost all unwritten; one of those priests

14 Sr. AGNESE of the Incarnate Word, born Barbara Schiavi (Corese 1757 - Rome 1810), an enclosed Minim nun of Saint Francis of Paola in the Rome monastery, which she entered as a lay sister. She advanced in the ways of God, graced with special charisms. Distinguished personages and humble people came to consult her, among them the Queen of Sardinia, Venerable Clotilde of Savoy, Saint Vincent Strambi and Mgr. Albertoni, to whom she foretold the founding of the Missionaries and Sisters of the Most Precious Blood by the priest (Saint) Gaspar del Bufalo.

ELISABETTA CANORI MORA (Rome 1774-1825). Wife and mother, a Trinitarian tertiary, she had charismatic gifts and suffered tribulations and passive purification together with diabolical vexations. Pius XI declared her virtues heroic on 26 Feb. 1928.

Blessed ANNA MARIA (Antonia Gesualda) TAIGI, née Giannetti (Siena 1769 - Rome 1837). At six she moved to Rome with her family; at eleven (1780) she made her First Communion in the then parish of Saint Francis of Paola ai Monti. Married from 1790, she was a Trinitarian tertiary and had gifts of heavenly locutions and clear knowledge of the present and future.

Venerable ELISABETTA SANNA (Codrongianos 1788 - Rome 1857). Wife and mother, then a widow, a Minim tertiary as well as Franciscan and Carmelite, also associated with Pallotti’s Society of the Catholic Apostolate. Docile to the Spirit, she advanced in Christian perfection. She came to Rome as a pilgrim in 1831 and stayed for twenty-five years, living on alms because of her poor health. Saint Vincent Pallotti was her spiritual director. She devoted herself entirely to works of charity.

Venerable GIOVANNI MERLINI (Spoleto 1795 - Rome 1873), of the Congregation of the Most Precious Blood, worked actively with Saint Gaspar del Bufalo in popular Missions.

“who hurried through the squares and narrow streets of the city…, anxious to reach a soul in need…; who advised the highest representatives of the Hierarchy, and who sometimes prepared a religious turning point for the whole of Christendom.”[15]

His presence in Rome in the first half of the nineteenth century stood for the primacy of faith and charity,[16] trust in God’s providence that never abandons,[17] the presence of the supernatural in the ministerial and charismatic service lavished on souls,[18] and the clear and explicit demonstration, dear to Saint Francis of Paola, Founder of the Minims, that nothing is impossible for one who loves God, but who loves him with unconditional fidelity and complete self-giving, in himself and in brothers and sisters undergoing trials.

Hospitals and prisons, religious communities including enclosed ones, individuals and families benefited from Clausi’s inner fervour and active zeal. A religious and priest “wholly God’s and fervent beyond belief in the things of the spirit”,[19] he walked long streets and climbed narrow stairs to advise, comfort and help, never tiring of others’ needs.

His actions revealed a living faith, the inner presence of the Spirit dwelling in him through divine grace, and the union of his will with God’s. So his life, interwoven with virtues and gifts in both the ordinary and the extraordinary, was a powerful presence, recalling the vital link between the witness of life and the faith professed, the special presence of the supernatural and God’s action in time.

When he shared maxims of devout life and spirituality, urged prayer and sacramental life, or spoke at all of spiritual and ascetical matters, Fr. Bernardo’s fervour and spiritual insight were captivating.[20] His words were already borne out by the Gospel example of his life. Add to this the comfort of God’s finger confirming his religious and priestly mission, enlightening minds and comforting hearts, strengthening their Christian faith and moving them to act accordingly. A sinner had only to manage to speak to him to feel changed and moved to change his life.[21] It was his virtue that convinced, more than the form of his words, which were in any case inspired.

In Rome, as earlier in Calabria and later elsewhere, Fr. Bernardo could have said, like the Apostle to the Corinthians, that he had come to bear witness to the truth of Christ “not with lofty words or wisdom”, “not with plausible words of human wisdom, but with a demonstration of the Spirit and of power”, so that the faith of those who saw him might rest “not on human wisdom but on the power of God”.[22] Indeed, one who was with him for nine years at Monti tells us:

“He was not a man of letters, because he had not followed the courses in the sciences… and because in the army he was forced to lose the most precious and suitable years for learning; yet when he spoke of spiritual things he was so wise in his reasoning and so rich in learning that he seemed a great theologian, so that the Reverend Fathers Lectors Br. Giovanni Villademont and Br. Francesco Pont… more than once said: ‘We are pygmies beside Fr. Bernardo Maria Clausi: we have studied and know nothing.’ And they concluded: ‘Ah, we have no doubt that Fr. Bernardo Maria Clausi has learned more by praying than we have by studying.’”[23]

His virtue was moreover marked by the seal of special charisms, which made it still more credible and persuasive and inspired imitation.

Attentive to the spiritual and temporal needs of others, Clausi was tireless in hearing confessions, preaching and helping in the most effective ways. He created spaces of faith and religious practice, of conformity to God’s will and of charitable initiatives. One could apply to him what the Samaritan woman’s fellow townspeople said of the Master of Nazareth:

“It is no longer because of what you said that we believe, for we have heard for ourselves and we know who he truly is.”[24]

In other words, the fact that he was a model of personal sanctification in the constant and exact fulfilment of his priestly and religious duty, with total acceptance of God’s will in faith and obedience, gave his presentation of Gospel truth, embodied in daily life and fidelity, the character of a convinced, attractive and imitable reality, in a witness who precisely as such became a teacher and evangelizer.

“For the Church,” as Pope Paul VI stated, “the first means of evangelization is the witness of an authentically Christian life, given over to God in a communion that nothing should destroy and at the same time given to one’s neighbour with limitless zeal.”[25]

From his return to Rome (but already during his first stay) until his final departure, this would be the meaning of Clausi’s residence, interspersed with journeys and temporary transfers. And elsewhere too it had the same meaning: that of the principles of Christian life proclaimed as fixed points, with the convincing witness of life and works, and confirmed by events even more convincing, of the same nature as those principles.

In October 1831 Fr. Bernardo arrived in Rome with an office that committed him first of all within the religious community he was to govern, and he would care for it with a zeal equal to the fervour of his observance. In vain he begged and implored the Vicar General not to confirm his election, considering himself unworthy of the merit his confreres saw in him. In vain he pointed out that, as during his earlier stay in Rome, the constant flow of people asking for his ministry, in the church there and elsewhere, might not allow him to keep proper watch over the reli-

Personally responsible

As a minister of God, bound to conform himself to Christ the Priest, essentially in divine worship and the service of souls, Fr. Bernardo, within the limits imposed on him, gave himself as usual to the loyal and generous fulfilment of his priestly and religious duties in the house and church at Monti. He was fully aware of being primarily responsible for the life of the local community, which had wanted him at its head, and he responded to the edification and benefit of others. He was first at all community acts. His dealings with his confreres matched his known virtues. He worked so that each religious might make progress in religious perfection and observance. He knew that the superior’s role is first of all to be a father and to go before the others in example and discipline, and, as the Rule of the Order says, to correct first himself and then, charitably, his brethren (hence the title Corrector), and he worked along these lines so admirably that he could have said, had he wished, with the Apostle: “Be imitators of me, as I [strive to be] of Christ.”[1] He led the way in constant prayer, punctuality and commitment to observance and ascetic discipline.[2]

With all the religious he had “most affable manners”, treating them “with extraordinary charity and deep humility”. He was well aware of the spirit of the Order and of what the disciplinary code appended to the Rule, the Correctorium, prescribes: that as superior he must consider himself in turn a “minim”, the least.[3] This came easily within his store of virtues.

Endowed with the qualities required in a superior, he was “respectful and most obedient towards his Major Superiors”,[4] but wanted no distinction or special deference for himself beyond what his office required, in the spirit of the Holy Founder, who, while inviting religious to “obey their superiors humbly” and honour them “with humble speech and respectful bearing”,[5] reminds each one who has done his duty: “after all these things, let them remember that they are unprofitable servants.”[6] He waited at table like the Brothers and helped them in their work in the sacristy, cleaning and refectory. By his example, fatherly care and discreet encouragement he promoted discipline and observance even among the less willing. When admonition was needed he gave it, but avoided intervening directly at the moment of the fault, preferring to see the culprit in private and, making him reflect on the harm done to himself and to common discipline, send him back to better observance with a playful compliment. A small admonition given this way was worth more than many harsh rebukes, and his confreres admitted that they profited more from it.[7]

If he noticed some disagreement or friction between religious, he called them to him and restored them to mutual charity. For breaches of silence at the times appointed for it and during work to be done in one’s room, he had a practical and discreet way of stopping them, together with those responsible. When he heard them, he would leave his room and start sweeping the stairs until they got the message and withdrew, without his having to say a word.[8]

At recreation, however, he wanted everyone to take honest relaxation, and with his cheerful, jovial manner he sometimes took the lead himself or was quick with a joke, helped by his humorous temperament.[9]

He had particular care and charity for sick religious, ready to serve them by day or watch over them at night if their condition required it.[10]

As for the promotion of divine worship,

Fr. Clausi had already given excellent proof of this at San Sisto, at Paola and here in Rome. He worked with renewed fervour for the beauty of the church, the celebrations and the sacred furnishings, by suitable means, ensuring that the church shone with cleanliness and decoration and that services were fitting and devout and, on special days and occasions, celebrated with due solemnity when required, urging religious and faithful, with words full of priestly zeal, to prepare properly. He himself prepared with love and heartfelt devotion[11] and celebrated with fervent virtue and prayer and every other ascetic quality. He was moved to this by the needs of his inner life, his personal consecration and deep conviction. A quick look at his theological life, beyond what we already know, confirms this. From the testimony in the processes later held on the holiness of his life, virtues and works, we learn that Fr. Clausi lived by faith, exercising it in almost continuous acts, even in particularly difficult circumstances.[12] He was ready to give his life for the faith,[13] and the acts and events, indications and signs of his deep faith are many. Besides his celebration of Mass and administration of the sacraments, wholly absorbed in their content of divine presence and grace, they include the sublime fervour and spiritual insight with which he habitually spoke of religion and spiritual and ascetical matters, especially the truths concerning the mysteries of the Most Holy Trinity and the Saviour’s Humanity, as if they were laid bare before the eyes of his mind,[14] or the privileges and prerogatives, mission and virtues of the Blessed Virgin and the Saints, particularly the Saint of

Paola, even creating opportunities to talk about them.[15]

His greatest opportunities came from the liturgical celebrations, rites and feasts of the liturgical year. In Holy Week an extraordinary recollection could be seen on his face, and, as people noticed, he seemed to be ill: he looked afflicted, crushed, exhausted. On Holy Saturday and in Easter week he seemed to have risen with Jesus, for his joy returned: he joked, sang, skipped about, did things that showed the gladness of his spirit, and spoke appropriately to stir up in his hearers gratitude and love for God for such great blessings. So too at Pentecost and on Marian feasts, when he seemed steeped in the mystery or solemnity being celebrated. His veneration for Our Lady was special.

“One only had to mention Our Lady,” Sr. M. Caterina Zanini would testify, “to see him almost rapt in ecstasy, or cheered and, I would say, almost carried away by the love that shone on his face.”[16]

In preparation for the feast of the Annunciation he generally invited people to consider that the Word became flesh, taking a human body, and suffered in it for love and the salvation of mankind; “a reason,” he said, “that should unite us to the sufferings of Jesus.” As Lent approached he would exclaim:

“Tristis est anima mea usque ad mortem; let us prepare to accompany Our Lord as he goes into the desert; let us keep him company.”[17]

This shows that his heart was wholly God’s and set on the things of Heaven.

His spirit of prayer and his life of prayer, to which he devoted his free moments too,[18] mark him out as a man of God and of prayer, in the highly significant role of a religious and priest who prays and leads others to pray.[19]

“He used to say,” a witness reports, “that our every breath should be in God and in the Blessed Virgin, and all our conversation with God and our guardian angel…”[20]

Indeed he was seen to be wholly steeped in God’s presence, centred on thought and love of him, always ready to do his will and acting for his glory.[21]

He often broke out in devotion before images of Jesus or Mary, the Cross and above all the Blessed Sacrament, which those who saw him called “his passion”.[22] He would turn to it, or to Our Lady, and lead others to do so, in all kinds of needs and requests for grace.[23]

“What are the goods of the world, after all?” he would ask. “Paradise, it is Paradise we must desire and seek, because it is the true good.” “O Paradise, O Paradise, how beautiful you are, and when shall I possess you?”[24] “We were created for Paradise. To aspire to that alone he had left the world and a position of prestige as curate-administrator.

Above his works, however, God’s charity in his mercy was the fundamental reason for his hope. Fr. Bernardo had a wonderful gift for urging and effectively moving people to trust in God, communicating steadfastness and calm in life’s various happy or sad events,[26] trust in God’s providence and mercy, and abandonment to his divine good pleasure.[27]

“We must never despair of God’s mercy,” he would observe, “nor ever abuse it, of course, for,” he would warn, “to sin in the hope of forgiveness is brazen presumption.”[28]

But charity towards God and neighbour was the centre and summit of Clausi’s theological life.

“When he spoke of God,” we are told, “his whole face lit up and he moved his hearers to great compunction”; likewise, “being with him was captivating because of his charity, affability and gentleness; he seemed to be out of this world.”[29] “Oh, if only everyone knew God!” he would exclaim;

and he prayed and had others pray that the Lord might be known, loved and adored.[30] In the fervour of celebrating Holy Mass his eyes not infrequently filled with tears.[31] Yet he remained himself even in his love of God, and at recreation he would sometimes hum devout tunes, saying that we must be cheerful and serve the Lord with gladness.[32] The truth is that he could not contain in his heart the overflowing wave of divine love. He was even subject to raptures of love for God, and would be surprised several times in such transports of charity, exclaiming: “O God who are Charity! O God who are Charity!…” or: “Ah, my God! My God who are Charity!”[33]

Fr. Bernardo’s charity towards God would be called “immense”, and towards his neighbour “indescribable”.[34] Let us now see how souls responded to such outstanding religious and priestly witness.

Besides churches, hospitals, prisons and monasteries were the places Fr. Bernardo visited most, bringing spiritual help and comfort. But he exercised a particular charity and ministry towards women religious, especially enclosed nuns, as confessor and counsellor, a trusted priest and experienced religious.

As we have said, first Gregory XVI and later Pius IX, besides often calling Clausi to them for their own edification and advice (especially the former), gave him permission to enter all monasteries freely to edify and comfort the consecrated souls living there.[87] The Church, rightly, for obvious reasons of esteem for and protection of contemplative life and those consecrated to it, has always jealously protected with very strict rules the papal enclosure of cloisters, as reserves of virgins consecrated to God and their Spouse, Jesus Christ. Such unlimited permission therefore shows the complete trust placed in Clausi as man, priest and religious, whose virtue and reputation for holiness were considered a proven guarantee. In the cholera of 1837

Back in Rome, Fr. Bernardo remained the man of prayer, the zealous priest and apostle, the Minim religious who was a perfect copy of the Founder, devoted to humility, charity and penance. Particular circumstances made him stronger still in each of these virtues and works.

His fervour in prayer, in its various private and liturgical forms, whether in the seclusion of his convent and cell or taking part in rites and celebrations, seemed undiminished despite the many demands of his priestly ministry. He knew how to harmonize outward activity with the inner need for prayer and constant asceticism, protecting himself with both from being swamped by activity. So he never lacked the necessary sap; indeed it grew as he ever more deeply interiorized the very motives and acts that, with indiscreet zeal, could easily have pulled him off centre.

As time went on, however, the influence of the gifts of the divine Spirit grew in his soul and, from supporting and strengthening his efforts at virtue and prayer, drove him towards higher goals of perfection. It was a matter of teachability to the voice and instruction of the Spirit, of docility in responding to it and of abandonment to his ways. Fr. Bernardo had long been trained in this.

From Mother Margherita Landi, who observed him directly from this time, we learn that the Father was habitually seen absorbed in God, as was clearly shown by the fact that even while talking he followed an inner thought of his own, not about earthly but heavenly things.[24] It was known that every day he went to the church of the Perpetual Adorers on Monte Cavallo, where he stayed a long time, recollected and kneeling in adoration of the Blessed Sacrament and reciting the penitential Psalms. He also attended the Forty Hours’ expositions.[25] When people looked for him they knew where to find him: usually praying in choir, church or his cell,[26] and not infrequently taking the discipline.[27]

In the street or at home, as soon as he left someone he returned at once to his inner prayer.[28] Clearly, then, his heart was ruled by a passion that held him fast, by a love that was not earthly: love for him who is more intimate to us than we are to ourselves. This was revealed by fiery sighs and groans and ardent aspirations heard from him as he walked or paused to pray.[29] An image or a devout reference would make him burst out in an exclamation of joy or a religious exhortation,[30] or he would take occasion “from even the smallest things to urge people to consider the power and goodness of God, who had drawn all creation out of nothing”.[31]

He used everything to rise to the love of God, whom he wanted loved and served by all, especially by religious and priests, because moved by that love they had given up everything for him; so the Lord’s faithfulness must be matched by theirs, called as they are to be holy and blameless in love.[32]

Fr. Domenico Rebecchi, his confrere, and others tell us that sometimes Clausi, to give vent to his burning love for the Lord without being noticed, would choose some lonely corner of the city, since he could not contain it except in church or in the open air.[33] At other times, to temper the “living flame of love” that enveloped him day and night, he would leave his cell and go to the choir, or walk barefoot in the dormitory, or go out onto the small loggia beside the bell tower, where, walking up and down with his arms raised in the form of a cross, he poured out irrepressible sighs:

“My God, how lovable you are; how good you are to me!” “My God, my Love!”[34]

If anyone noticed and asked him what was the matter, he would answer simply:

This did not distract him from his priestly and religious duties, especially confessions, visits to the sick and community acts; in them, indeed, his only aim was the love of God and the good of souls.[36] He proved this superlatively in what has sadly gone down in history as the year of the cholera in Rome.

The terrible epidemic had already swept across Europe from Russia to Spain, and Hungary, Austria and France had lost many lives, as had other countries. In Italy the deadly contagion began in Livorno and claimed its first victims on 13 September 1835. Neither the states and peoples of the North nor those of the South were spared, as the death toll advanced relentlessly. The sanitary cordons set up here and there, including in the Papal States, were of little or no use. In a penitential pilgrimage ordered by the Pope on 8 September 1835, the image of Our Lady “Salus Populi Romani” was carried in procession from the Borghese Chapel of the Liberian Basilica to Saint Peter’s and then brought back to Saint Mary Major, followed by clergy and faithful led by Gregory XVI himself, barefoot and in penitential garb.[37] But

Rome too was assailed, from the coast and along inland routes, though not until 1837. In just two weeks, from 27 August to 9 September, some 3,000 died of “cholera morbus”. Many hurried to leave the city; others sought safety by shutting themselves up at home. A month later the total number of victims had almost doubled, though the daily rate had fallen. On 9 September Clausi wrote to his friend Caterini in Naples: “The cholera has somewhat lessened (sic).”[38] At last it stopped on 12 October.[39]

Already fearing the relentless approach of the disease, the capital had lived in anguish and dread. Many had commended themselves to Clausi’s prayers and asked for his charity and advice. Fr. Fr. Bernardo saw this “visitation” and the end of the scourge as the time of the Lord’s “new mercies” or “longed-for mercies”, of which he declared himself “certain”. He had written a year earlier:

“I hope God’s new mercies are so near that I believe they have already come; let us be of good heart, for we shall see great and most consoling things that cannot be explained at all.”[44]

Then on 8 July, as that time of God’s “mercy” drew near, writing to the superior of the Minims of the Stella in Naples, he had written even more clearly:

“I shall make it my duty to pray to the Lord for you and for everyone, and especially that he hasten his new mercies, for unless it begins from Heaven our heads and hearts cannot be set right. Self-offering as a victim and the first spiritual trials

His letters allow us to follow Fr. Bernardo in the years after the cholera until his journey to Piedmont, from 1838 to 1842: four years and some months spent uninterruptedly in Rome, apart from twenty days in October 1841 when he went for the third time to the Holy House of Loreto and to some other places in the Marches.[48]

He continued to await the long-desired general mercies and consolations from God. The “concordat” also continued, that is, his offering of himself for this; so he told one of the souls he directed that “the Lord has been moved to compassion for us all”, and he still hoped “at any moment for the long-awaited graces, mercies and spiritual consolations”.[49]

“I tell you in great haste that our holy, most holy, sacrosanct (sic) concordat is going very well against that ugly, most ugly beast Don Peppino, for the Lord has been moved to compassion for us all, and I hope at any moment for the long-awaited graces,

And yet, in keeping with his self-offering as a victim, while others, to whom his zeal and priestly ministry, his charity and prayerful intercession were directed, experienced God’s consolations, and he foretold still greater ones, for Clausi himself a long spiritual trial began: first inner darkness, then ever sharper tribulation. By his own account there are clear signs of it in a letter of direction from December 1838. God had accepted the offering and the host was becoming a sacrifice. Clausi was fully aware of this and shared it joyfully.

“God’s beautiful mercies, so necessary for us and so longed for,” he wrote, “will come without any doubt, for he has shown and promised them countless times to Fr. Bernardo and to many other servants of his. But now I would not know what to tell you, for I have been in thick darkness for five months, and not only I but everyone. Let us pray that he make haste, for things are hard now.”[51]

In fact, ever since May 1833 Clausi had experienced alternating trials and consolations, after a whole year of intense spiritual consolation. This is how he confided it to Fr. Giovan Battista Mantuano in February 1849, as they passed along what is now Via della Polveriera in Rome:

“On the feast of Saint Pius V, 5 May 1832, I went to visit him in his chapel at Saint Mary Major, and after a short prayer I remembered that the Forty Hours’ exposition was on at Saint John Lateran, so I decided to go and make my visit there. There I was so seized by holy love that I no longer felt able to converse with people: my mind [was] absorbed in God; both in the College and in the streets I could not contain my love, and I had to give vent to it at night in the open air and by day in these open fields. No harsh weather could stop me, and the iciest frosts were tempered by the fire of love that the Lord deigned to grant me from that day until the same day of the following year, 1833.”

Then came the ups and downs, adversities mingled with consolations, which he always bore courageously as trials sent by God.[52]

Of these trials he confided to Fr. Giacomo Colombi of the Lazarists, again in January 1838 [sic; note 53 gives 1839]:

“I gladly pray to God for everyone, living and dead, but on everything else I would not know what to answer you, for I am in great darkness. We must always hope for good from the Lord, for he is an Almighty and Merciful Father, but the things he has reserved to himself he seldom reveals.”[53]

In March of the same year he confirmed the same prophetic line of “extraordinary graces and new mercies of God for all”.

“Be more than sure,” he added, “… for God is faithful and cannot lie in his promises. Let others say what they will… but Fr. Bernardo, in spite of his enormous pride, his cursed self-love, his ignorance and his cursed sins, assures you on God’s behalf that the consolations the Lord is preparing for us will be so many and so great that Heaven itself will be astonished as it gazes on and admires the great work of the Most High…”[54]

A year later he restated his inner experience:

“Now is a time of very great darkness and gloom, and it is general… What I have always written and said to everyone I shall go on saying, for these are the things I have always known [the divine mercies], and never punishments…”[55]

The prophetic announcement became more explicit as to its scope too. Behind it lay an event described as follows: a vision of a sky covered with thick clouds and a tremendous crash like thunder that seemed to resound throughout the world, followed in a moment by a clear sky and a very great light. Valuable help for the parish of San Sisto

The wait for these mercies of the Lord continued into 1841[59] and beyond, though explicit references became rarer, as Clausi, besides his usual religious and priestly ministry, gave valuable help to the general restoration, “almost from the foundations”,[60] and the renewal of the furnishings and sacred vessels of the parish church of his native town.[61] His help was valuable because of the benefactors he approached and the money and goods entrusted to him that he could send for this purpose and for the poor in general.[62]

Among the most illustrious benefactors were King Charles Albert of Sardinia and his Foreign Minister, Count Clemente Solaro della Margarita, to whom in gratitude he sent some devotional objects from the Loreto Sanctuary through Count Broglia, minister of the Royal House to the Holy See,[63] as well as Duke Marino Torlonia and various other distinguished admirers.[64]

To forestall exaggerated demands from his fellow townspeople, however, Clausi made clear that what he did and obtained purely for the love of God did not make him powerful, nor should it make him indiscreet.

Of Charles Albert, the “Magnanimous” King of Sardinia (Turin 1798 – Oporto 1849), of the Savoy-Carignano branch, it is known that although brought up in a revolutionary and Napoleonic setting and restored to his homeland by the Restoration, he had a clear sense of the State and a genuine religious spirit, while being open to necessary reforms. Coming to the throne in 1831 as heir presumptive on the death of Charles Felix, he had already shown he no longer sympathized with the rebels and set about a cautious reformism, standing firm in defence of the Catholic religion, sincerely supported in this by his Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Clemente Solaro della Margarita. Only later, under pressure from a new government of liberal and Masonic leanings, after granting the Statute as the State’s fundamental constitutional charter (1848), which it would remain for almost a century, did he allow himself to be pushed into war against Austria in pursuit of irredentist and national dreams. He was politically overwhelmed by the defeat at Novara, abdicated in favour of his son Victor Emmanuel and went into exile in Oporto. Judgement of his honesty as a man and his authenticity as a Christian and devoted son of the Church is not invalidated by political influences stronger than himself or by the military and diplomatic complications of which he was the first victim.

On Clausi’s prophecies, we have already mentioned his allusions, in letters and orally, to prophetic knowledge concerning trials and tribulations of the Church, to be followed by extraordinary consolations and graces, all of which he constantly included under the name of “the Lord’s mercies”.[42] During this stay outside the Papal States, too, Fr. Bernardo occasionally spoke of them. Among other things, when the Prior of the Dominicans at Saint Vincent’s, Racconigi, asked him whether times would remain normal, or as they were, or not, he answered with a troubled face:

“Oh, Father Prior, some days ago, on the feast day (I no longer remember of which Saint, notes the writer) I had something like a vision that foretold very troubled times for the Church, but for now I can say no more.” Then he added: “Let us hope in God’s infinite mercy,” and fell silent.[43]

Ministry in Rome and new apostolic journeys

Bernardo Clausi’s apostolic journeys closely resemble those of Saint Francis of Paola, God’s wayfarer on the roads of men. He too, a man of God, alternated travel with longer or shorter stays, renewing the witness of faith and gospel service and promoting spiritual and moral renewal. Like the holy Founder of the Minims, he had this charism and was a sign of it.

The Paterno mission

Many wonders had occurred during the building of this convent in the Saint of Paola’s time, perhaps even more than at Paola, his home town. It was therefore called the “Convent of Miracles”, and many are recorded in witnesses’ sworn depositions in the processes for the canonization of Saint Francis.[37]

After some four centuries the convent had shared the fate of others closed under the suppression laws that followed the French occupation of the Kingdom of Naples. Despite the Bourbon restoration it had not yet been reopened; so after the steps taken for the Paola Sanctuary, the necessary procedures had begun to have Paterno returned to the Order of Minims too. Since 1840, however, they had been stuck in the bureaucracy. A single intervention by Clausi, asked by his confreres, was enough: through his plea, to God before men, and a letter to the Neapolitan Minister of the Interior, the Marquis Santangelo, the desired royal decree was ready.[38] But this was only the beginning of his work for the Paterno Sanctuary. Much remained to be done to restore God’s house and the dwelling of those consecrated to him.

The return of the sacred buildings to the Minims, rather than their formal reopening, took place in the second half of July 1845.[39] Fr. Bernardo went there two months later[40] and stayed two years, charged with restoring the buildings and serving as Vicar Corrector of the re-established community. This could not be done quickly, given the dilapidated and neglected state of the premises and load-bearing structures. But trust and enterprising zeal overcame his initial dismay. Fr. Luigi Martini, one of his first three confreres at Paterno and formerly his neighbour in the next cell at the Monti in Rome,[41] reports:

The first works began, and gradually there was a ferment of activity. Bernardo did directly, renewing the experience of the first building of the old hermitage. Dozens of people, men and women of various kinds, gave their labour out of charity; others were paid; all worked with zeal and commitment worthy of the cause. Contractor, agent and factotum for ordering materials and putting them in place: Clausi himself.[44]

As the first restoration progressed, the church could function again, and devotees of Saint Francis of Paola from the hamlets of Paterno and the surrounding villages and towns came on pilgrimage. Not only the restored places of the Saint but Fr. Bernardo’s virtue and effective ministry drew people in faith and trust in the supernatural.

“You cannot imagine the great crowds at this Sanctuary, which seems an earthly Paradise,” he told a devout benefactress in Rome.[45]

Naturally Clausi and his confreres had twice as much spiritual and sacramental care to give, at great cost of time and physical energy, which tried his health so much that the Father felt the need for some rest and proper treatment.

“From the moment I arrived at this Sanctuary I have never had a minute’s time,” he wrote in April 1846, “both because of the restoration of this holy house and because of the crowds for confession. When the work is over I hope to have a little quiet.”[46] The “work”, in this case on the Sanctuary, “is well advanced in about six months, whereas it should have taken at least six years”, given the state it was found in.[47]

In fact his sacred ministry was not confined to Paterno but extended to the surrounding districts and towns, visiting the sick and helping the poor, since there was famine throughout the province of Cosenza.[48] Dipignano, Rende, San Fili, Montalto, San Benedetto Ullano, Grimaldi and others called for him, and not infrequently faith and charity were crowned by a miracle.[49]

Fr. Bernardo did not dare refuse, and Don Vincenzo Plantedi, who usually went with him, would testify that when he went “with him to various villages near Paterno for the good of our neighbour” he was always prompt and recollected, as if to make up in intensity the time the apostolate took from pure and simple prayer. “Along the way,” he would say, “he did not make idle conversation with me but was always absorbed in contemplating heavenly things, and with such elevation of spirit that he seemed not to walk but to fly, and I, who was neither old nor infirm, had trouble keeping up with him.”[50]

Imagine, then, what apostolic energy! Not that he lacked time and quiet altogether: time he took at night while all were asleep, keeping vigil at least in part and feeding on prayer and the discipline. Quiet and rest, apart from what the nature around the Sanctuary offered, he felt a more pressing need of. But here too intensity made up for length, helped by Fr. Bernardo’s indomitable will and generous heart, which were comforted by special supernatural help and gifts.

On 29 January 1846, after celebrating Mass and praying with intense fervour, he went out to the place called u maricieddu[51] and was found there rapt in ecstasy, raised from the ground almost to a man’s height.[52] A sign that the man’s inner commitment was ready to receive both the ordinary and extraordinary call of grace. Yet his growing hunger and thirst for God and his longing for union made him want at least occasional returns to solitude to be alone with him: the ancestral need, the fatherly temperament inherited from the holy Minims, the call to the “desert” to prepare for the fullness of God.

At Paterno the places of the Saint of Paola, the cave and oratory, the furnace of the miracle, the shrines of the black mulberry and the chestnut trees, also linked to Saint Francis’ miracles, and the church, cloister, countryside and mountains, are full of atmosphere and mysticism;[53] but the coming and going of pilgrims and the constant ministry it required limited Clausi’s hours of prayer and checked his fervour. Although the community grew to about ten fathers and brothers, and “everyone was happy… and there was observance and discipline”,[54] his inner call grew sharper and more pressing. So Fr. Bernardo thought of withdrawing for a while to the convent of Pozzano at Castellammare di Stabia, but he kept having to postpone the trip, and even when he managed to go, about a year later on his way to Rome, he could not at once give himself fully to it nor restore his health at the famous local spa.[55] He had to cut short both the stay and its purpose.[56]

What spiritual masters unanimously call passive purification is found in Clausi, in an alternation of love and suffering, not without the tribulation he felt acutely at precisely this time. If on the one hand he would be consumed by the purifying trial suited to his temperament, his charisms and his personal self-offering as a victim, on the other God’s work would be exalted in him. We shall see its triumph and the crowning of his heroic fidelity, a fidelity in which he is again a particular witness and sign. Then the appearance of divine abandonment, which is part of the purifying experience, would reveal its true nature as full conformity to the image of the Father’s beloved Son in his similar experience on the Cross. The hour of his trial

For Clausi it was a long and painful hour, of anguish of spirit and sadness, of the power of darkness and passion, of agony and death; but also of heroic faith, of hope against hope, of consuming love of God and neighbour.

At the height of the purifying trial comparisons follow thick and fast: with holy Job, the prophet Jonah and Jeremiah, and the apostle Paul, who said he was ready to be accursed and cut off from Christ if only his brethren might be saved; above all, with Christ crucified and in agony, and in the Cross the sign of divine predilection is evident. There are also apocalyptic notes and references to the infernal dragon and the beast, to the battle between spirits and the victory of Michael the Archangel over the Evil One, in a lucid sequence culminating in the triumph marked by the Ambrosian hymn to the One and Triune God, in whose echo Clausi’s soul found its complete liberation and took its final flight towards eternity.

Let us follow the experience of this terrible hour, both in the events that prepared it and in the one that marked its beginning. Here is what was almost the first blow, as confided by Clausi himself.

In May 1847 Fr. Bernardo left Paterno to return to Rome. Reaching Naples, he stopped there, as we know, to repay his debt of gratitude to various benefactors who had contributed to the radical restoration of the Paterno Sanctuary. It was in the summer months of that year[11] that, begged and urged to meet people’s spiritual needs, he went to Castellammare di Stabia and Sorrento.[12] There he celebrated Mass and then, as was his custom, served another priest’s Mass. The people, seeing him kneeling at the foot of the altar, recognized him and, moved by the fame of his extraordinary virtues, could not restrain their esteem and veneration. They approached him one after another, then in a swarm, some to kiss the image of the “Madonnina” he carried, some his hand, some the hem of his habit.

“It was then,” Fr. Luigi Martini would testify, having later been told by him, “that Fr. Bernardo, to stop the noise made by the crowd, left the altar to hide in the sacristy.”[13]

But it was useless, for they followed him, causing some crush and inevitable noise. The celebrant was so indignant that when Mass was over and he returned to the sacristy he began to rail at Clausi, sarcastically calling him a hypocrite, a fraud, an abuser of people’s good faith and the like. Those present were indignant in turn, because the rebukes were unjust, while the Father was the only one not to lose his serenity and usual good humour. In his humility, however, he took the unpleasant episode and the names he had been called to heart, and gradually resolved to return to Paterno

He had not yet carried it out when a new episode in Naples, together with the previous one, deeply shook his spirit and filled him with anxiety and fear.

His passing through and temporary stay in the city could not go unnoticed, and in an indiscreet excess of veneration people not only acclaimed him a saint but nearly stripped him of his habit to share it out as relics. Fr. Bernardo, out of scruple over self-love or vainglory, although on such occasions he would usually repeat to the Lord, deeply humbled, “Tibi gloria, mihi confusio”,[15] went and threw himself at the feet of a confessor.[16] To nip such temptations in the bud, the confessor suggested he destroy letters and papers from eminent persons addressed to him, which he had kept until then,

“not out of vanity but in memory of those people and to show his gratitude by commending them to the Lord”.[17]

But the flea of pride put in his ear and the fear of having fallen victim to it unawares increased his spiritual anguish. “This thought was my inseparable companion”;[18] and he decided to withdraw at once to Paterno. To his deputy in that community he wrote:

So he left and put into practice his resolve of greater austerity and hiddenness, giving himself to still more assiduous prayer and harsh penance, never ceasing to ponder the eternal truths.

“Meditation, prayer, spiritual reading, fasting, the discipline and every kind of the strictest mortification were his life. Meanwhile Clausi was awaited in Rome, and his Superior General urged his return, also at the Pope’s wish. So in the second half of November he left the Paterno Sanctuary for good. The local community wanted to keep him longer, but he pointed out that obedience called him elsewhere and it was his duty to obey.

He reached Paola on Tuesday evening, before 18 November, and learned that the brethren of the Sanctuary community “had long since petitioned the Father General”[24] to have him as their Superior, an office and offer that Fr. Bernardo was ready to decline, not feeling equal to it, though ready in this too for God’s will.[25] But God wanted him in Rome, as we shall see, and he resumed his journey. He reached Naples on the night of the Saturday before 29 November, after an eventful voyage on the “Duca di Calabria”,[26]

“because,” he explained to those at Paterno, “off the coast at Licosa (sic) the steamer was in danger at 7 o’clock at night, through the carelessness of the man at the helm, and we escaped by the grace of Most Holy Mary and were delayed about 10 hours.”[27]

Still in Naples, or more probably in nearby Castellammare at the Pozzano Sanctuary,[28] a new event struck Fr. Bernardo with more violent inner repercussions.[29]

He had gone there to make a strict spiritual retreat. He had just begun it when,

“while he was praying,” a witness with direct knowledge would testify, “he heard a horrible voice. He raised his eyes and saw an iron ring” (“as if red-hot”, another witness specifies[30]) “and a voice like thunder said to him: ‘This is for you.’” Or, in another version he confided: “Whether you do or don’t, it is all over for you, because you are lost.”[31]

It was the first brazen assault of the father of lies to strike terror and despair into him. At this voice and vision,[32] Clausi confided to Fr. Mantuano,

“I burst into painful tears and believed from then on that I was abandoned by God.”[33]

Fr. Bernardo was no stranger to spiritual desolation,[34] but the desolation that followed these events marked the violent beginning of his great tribulation. In God’s light, the light of dark contemplation, as Saint John of the Cross would say, which God gives to enlighten and purify from habitual natural and spiritual ignorance and imperfections,[35] one sees darkness and suffers deep pain and affliction. So he hurried back to Naples and from there left at once for Rome.

Rome awaits and welcomes him

During Clausi’s long absence important events had taken place in Rome, above all the death of Gregory XVI and the election of the new Pope.

After sixteen years as Pope, aged 81, Gregory XVI died on Whit Monday, 1 June 1846. The positive side of his pontificate in the strictly religious and spiritual sphere, such as the reorganization of the hierarchy, the reform of the ancient religious orders, the approval of many new institutes of perfection and the planting of the Church in vast new mission lands, cannot be underestimated, still less ignored, because his temporal administration of the State was less successful.[36]

All in all, during his reign this Pope had done what he could, facing the various revolutionary uprisings that by now broke out here and there chronically. The political legacy he left his successor was certainly not an easy one. Yet precisely because the new Pope was seen as liberal-leaning,[37] the beginning of his pontificate was hailed with vibrant enthusiasm.

Pius IX, Giovanni Maria Mastai-Ferretti, elected on 16 June 1846 in a conclave lasting only two days, was crowned on the 21st. Less than a month later, on 16 July, he granted a broad amnesty to political prisoners. At the same time he set about repairing the shortcomings of the previous temporal administration and allowed exiles to return. So from the start he aroused enormous interest in Italy and Europe.

“Such a man,” wrote D’Azeglio, “has done more for Italy in two months than all Italians have done in twenty years.”[38]

But not all the enthusiasm shown him by the crowds, who kept up ovations and demonstrations of support for the various political concessions, was sincere.[39]

Count Solaro della Margarita, who came to Rome to pay homage to the new Pope, informed Charles Albert that the popular excitement concealed ulterior motives.[40] The “hosannas” in the square were skilfully orchestrated by liberals and radicals to force the Pope’s hand, and when he held back, those same people would whip the excitement up to the well-known upheavals of 1848. But let us return to Clausi. “Will he come back to Rome?” “Whenever Your Holiness wishes,” was the reply.
